toc.title: How shutdown shows up in someone you love
When shutdown doesn't look like shutdown

blocks.p: A dorsal vagal shutdown is one of three primary autonomic states. It occurs when one can't exist in their ventral vagal safety state, and when sympathetic flight and fight haven't worked. The body collapses, or plays dead at the extreme. It's a normal biological reaction in the face of a life threat.

But we can get stuck in a dorsal vagal shutdown. Day to day, it shows up in our emotions, our thoughts, our behaviors, and even our connections with others. It directly impacts our life, our happiness, and our motivation. You likely have somebody in your life who is stuck in shutdown. Maybe somebody at your work, or even in your own home. Heck, you may be stuck in shutdown yourself. But here I'm going to focus on how to recognize it in others, because when we recognize shutdown in others, it might help us to feel more compassion and less judgment for them.
Biologically, shutdown is a state of immobilization. Specifically, collapsed and limp. Freeze is also a state of immobilization, but tense.

Shutdown is also a state of conservation. The body is slowing down, or shutting down, its processes to conserve resources in anticipation of coming out of shutdown. When it comes out of shutdown, it emerges into sympathetic flight and fight activation, and then uses that energy to create space, escape, and return to safety.

Shutdown also requires reduced stimulation. The external world is overwhelming. It's too much. Shutdown needs less: less noise, less light, even fewer people. On that note, shutdown is usually pretty alone. In shutdown, one disconnects from others, and even from themselves to some degree.
So let's understand shutdown as a state of collapsed and disconnected immobilization.

Is what I'm going to share true for everyone all the time? Of course not. But these are fairly predictable presentations of shutdown. At the end, I'll throw a wrench into everything and share how shutdown can look completely different.

blocks.h: How shutdown shows up in someone you love

blocks.p: Someone in shutdown, including your loved one, may withdraw. They might be isolating themselves. This can be as extreme as locking themselves in a dark room and doom scrolling for hours, or oversleeping. Being alone feels better for somebody who's in shutdown. Other people are potentially overwhelming. Not to mention the sounds, the crowds, and the lighting of the places we typically go every day.

You might go to the grocery store and have no problem. But someone in shutdown could struggle to get out of their front door because they're so physically exhausted. And when they get to the store, getting through that next door might be another huge challenge. Remember, shutdown is a state of collapse. Their body is prepared to collapse, not to mobilize and go to the store. And if they make it to the store, they could legitimately struggle with overstimulation: too many people, too many sights, too many sounds, lighting that's too harsh.

You might think, "Well, too bad. They need to get over it," or "That's an excuse for laziness." I'm not asking you to be okay with the shutdown your loved one is struggling with. I'm not asking you to be okay with how they're handling it, or not handling it. I don't think the person in shutdown is okay with it either. But whether you accept it or not, these are potential obstacles for somebody in shutdown. This is their reality, or at least a piece of it.

When someone is stuck in shutdown, you'll see it in their face and their body. Shutdown is about collapse, so someone in shutdown will have a collapsed look to them. Maybe not lying on the floor, literally collapsed, but slumped, slouched, shriveled. They appear smaller. This is how they show up to my therapy office, no matter what age they are, honestly. Teens are probably more obvious about it, but adults do it too. As mobility comes back into their system, they can sit upright and lean forward, and they think and plan with more motivation and more intention.

Somebody in shutdown will also have unique facial qualities, and by unique I mean they kind of don't have facial qualities. They still have faces, obviously, but the life in their face is just kind of gone. They're flat. There's no emotion in their faces. They don't smile. Their eyes are open, but only partially, especially compared to flight and fight, where they're more wide open. Their upper cheeks aren't doing much, and eye crinkles don't really form at the corners of their eyes. Of course, I'm speaking very generally, and really more to the extreme, one-dimensional presentation of shutdown. There's a variety of possible presentations, but you're likely to see these types of things.

When you're with someone who's in shutdown, you might feel yourself pulled down, heavier, less hopeful. It's not their fault. They're not imposing that feeling on you. You, as an empathetic, caring person, are feeling a bit of what it's like to be them. That's a bit of their experience, day in and day out.

Someone in shutdown also hugely struggles with eye contact. They tend to look down. In flight and fight, we look away also, but more around the environment, almost scanning for danger. Or in flight and fight, our eyes are wider open, staring at the person in front of us and maybe even creating uncomfy eye contact.

But in shutdown, they look down, like they lack the energy to even look up. Maintaining eye contact is pretty much impossible, because it requires a lot of safety in the system. So if you're someone who needs eye contact to feel listened to and understood, you're kind of out of luck. If the body is in a state of collapse and thinks its life is in threat, then making eye contact and facial emotiveness are just not priorities for that body.

In shutdown, the voice becomes flat, just like facial affect and body posture. It's there, but there's no life in it. Very monotone, and leaning more into the deeper end of the vocal spectrum, no matter what their gender is.

In safety, we have something called vocal prosody, which is a sing-songy quality of voice. Vocal prosody enables us to go high and low, and it allows us to express our emotions and our intent through our voice. In a defensive state, that's not really possible. Shutdown in particular, as a defensive state, is flat in prosody. It's also slower. There isn't much energy in what someone in shutdown is saying. Sometimes it even seems like they struggle to get through the sentence.

It's not uncommon for someone in shutdown to think before they speak, inhale, and then say one sentence that bypasses everything that was being talked about. For example, if you ask someone in shutdown what motivates them, they might pause, breathe in, and then say, "What's the point?" That one sentence may be the best they can muster.

Just like the face and the voice, thinking in shutdown is flat, devoid of energy, not much life in it. Very pessimistic. Lacking hope. Helpless, even. Again, this is at the extreme. Someone in shutdown can totally have a job they excel at, but outside that context, they fall into typical shutdown experiences. Or when they're in a different environment, like nature, or with a loved one, or with their pet in silence, they're less shut down, more mobile, and maybe even more hopeful.

In shutdown, the body is preparing to die, so thinking is not a priority, just like facial emotions, vocal prosody, and body posture. Everything is slowing down, including thoughts, and the ability to form new memories, to sustain attention, to think critically, and to think with hope and motivation.

You might think, "Well, they just need to think more positively." And yeah, you're right. I don't exactly disagree. But it's also not going to happen, at least not while they're in shutdown. When we're in a defensive state, we don't have access to all of our brain functions. That includes flight, fight, freeze, and shutdown, but in shutdown we might have even less. At the very extreme, someone in shutdown may actually dissociate. They may disconnect from their bodies, from reality, and from you. They don't want to. It's not a conscious choice. It's a biological reaction that affects the entire body, including the brain.
The collapsed state of shutdown affects how your loved one feels, too. In shutdown, the individual feels slow, empty, heavy. What else would they feel if they were ready to collapse and play dead?

They potentially feel hopeless and helpless as well. They also know they're letting people down, and themselves too. They know they're not fulfilling their responsibilities, or that they're wasting their life to some degree. So they also feel guilt and regret, maybe even shame. There's an overall sense of disconnection in shutdown, and it shows up emotionally in a bunch of ways.

blocks.h: When shutdown doesn't look like shutdown

blocks.p: Here's the wrench. Someone in shutdown may adopt behaviors that completely mask the fact that they're in shutdown. This is more for those who are in life contexts where they're dealing with abuses of various kinds day in and day out.

Someone who's been repeatedly abandoned, neglected, or let down seriously lacks safe connections, and they may need to become someone else to meet their own survival needs. They're still them, but they're them with a fake smile on their face. They may behave in ways that seem counterintuitive to their well-being, like connecting with their abusers, something that's called appeasement. Or they may preemptively attempt to reduce their partner's rage by prioritizing the partner's needs, through something called fawning.
So what the heck do you do about all this? You're a caring individual in this person's life. You hate seeing them go through this.

You don't have to be okay with someone being in shutdown. You don't have to be okay with the choices they make from shutdown. You don't have to think it's forever, and you don't have to think you're helpless in the face of it. You're allowed to want better for them. They want it, too. I'm not telling you how you should or should not act or feel in response to your loved one's shutdown. But here are four steps I recommend.

Acknowledge the potential truth of the situation. In other words, validate it. Validating means acknowledging what is true. If what I've described sounds like your loved one, just acknowledge it. That doesn't mean being okay with it or liking it. Just acknowledge it.

If you brought your validation to that person, it would probably be more beneficial to them than telling them to think differently or reminding them that they're wasting their life. They already know.

After validating, the next thing you can do is normalize. That means you reflect on their life and ask yourself, "If I had their life, would I likely have a similar shutdown response?" Or, "If somebody else had their life, would they likely have a similar shutdown response?"

For example, if your spouse who suffered ongoing abuse as a child is in shutdown, does that make sense? If your friend whose parents abandoned him when he was young is in shutdown, does that make sense? If your coworker lost those closest to her this past year, would it make sense why she's in shutdown? If your parents were raised in an extremely controlling and publicly shaming religious institution, would it make sense why they might be in shutdown?
Normalizing doesn't mean being okay with it. It doesn't mean liking it. It just means making sense of it.

If their shutdown is valid and normal, the next step is to let it be. Stop fighting it. Stop minimizing it. Stop excusing it. Stop denying it. Let them be in shutdown. Again, you don't have to be okay with it or like it.

Letting them be in shutdown means you let go of control, or the illusion of control. It's their shutdown, not yours, so let them have it. You can still expect the best of them. You can still hope for the best for them. You can still hold them accountable for the choices they make, or don't make. But it's their shutdown, and it's up to them, ultimately, to get themselves out of it.
Of course, you want to help them, and you can. After validating, normalizing, and letting them be in shutdown, you can connect with them more meaningfully.

Deb Dana has this wonderful analogy for connecting with somebody in shutdown, which she got from somebody else. Someone in shutdown is like a turtle inside its shell. If you want the turtle to come out, you don't knock on the shell and shake it and force it to come out. Instead, you sit patiently and wait. She put it this way when she was on the podcast:

q: To get a turtle to come out of the shell, you don't knock on its shell and you don't shake them... You just kinda sit there patiently... But you really have to be beaming that ventral vagal energy to that system.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.p: Your loved one is in their shutdown shell. Begging, pleading, yelling, forcing, threatening, shaming, guilt tripping: these things won't help. They may actually make things worse. I would kind of bet on it, in all honesty. Instead, be patient and wait for them to come out.

You can also want the best for them. You can tell them you believe in them, that you love them, that you want them to get professional support. But part of the equation in helping them is to give them patience. Another part is to give them space. They don't do well with pressure and pushing. They may need space, or if you're with them, they may do better with quiet and calm. Maybe ask them. They might know.
Does this mean you give them space and let them indulge in isolation, time killing, and ignoring responsibilities? Of course not.

I was working with a young man who had just completed high school and failed his first year of college. He was living with his parents, isolating in his room, no job, not in school, lots of video game time, and time with his girlfriend and his friends. He wasn't doing house chores. In every way, this young man was shut down. He was pretty unmotivated, wracked with guilt and shame and regret. He was pretty deep in shutdown, I would say.

His parents did what any typical parent would do. They pressured, they pleaded, they begged, they fought, and they also judged him. All of it came from love. I know it sounds weird, but they wanted the best for him, and they were having a hard time watching him in shutdown, wasting away, pretty much. All of their efforts didn't help, and they probably solidified his shutdown even more. Even though it was ineffective, it came from the best place, and it came from love. They just didn't know how to connect with him, or how to help him get to that next step.

Things got so bad for him that he sought out therapy, because he knew he needed help and things were looking pretty dim. But instead of connecting with me directly, he asked his parents to find him a therapist, and they connected with me. They all came to the first session, and it went really well. He was supposed to come work with me one on one, but the next session, he flaked.

Because he was rude? No. Because he was insensitive, or because he didn't care about his life? No. He's in shutdown. Following through, feeling motivated, feeling energized enough to get out of the house a second time was too much for him.

So we didn't give up. We didn't shame him. The parents didn't judge him. His parents and I worked together on how to best help him meet his goals. They knew what didn't work, so we focused on what might work. They did a combination of a few things:

ol: They gave him more statements of love, support, and encouragement.
They reduced how many statements of negativity they gave him. Was it easy and smooth? Heck no. But they did good enough.
They told him that if he couldn't complete his household expectations, like taking the garbage out, then he would not be able to use their electricity for things like video games.

blocks.p: They told him he could make his own choices. They would not hound him, and they would not pressure him. They would simply remove the privileges they had provided to him that he had not earned. The electricity for video games was a privilege they gave him even though he didn't earn it.

All of these pieces helped him reduce his isolation and connect with his parents more. He also came back to therapy and worked with me one on one to boost his motivation and start getting things done. He wanted to get things done. He was just in a deep shutdown and didn't know what to do next. We met individually, I think once, and after that meeting, he started applying to jobs, he re-enrolled in school, and he and I even met with his dad so they could talk some things out. They had some issues between the two of them that had been ignored for years and years.

The parents gave him love and support, but more effectively: without the guilting and the shaming. And instead of watching him not live up to their expectations, or his own expectations of himself, they changed something else. They removed the privileges they were giving him that he had not earned. So they gave him love and support, and plenty of time to make his own decisions, while also influencing his decision making by removing privileges when it was appropriate.

That three-part setup, increasing positivity, decreasing negativity, and granting privileges only when they're earned, was way more helpful than begging, pleading, trying to convince him, hounding him, and pressuring him. Once they removed the friction of themselves from his shutdown, he got the space, the incentive, and the support to decide on his own to change his life.
Before you attempt to do anything differently, it may help to reflect on whatever feelings you have about doing something different.

ul: When the thought of giving them more space is in your head, how do you feel about that?
If you typically pressure someone who's in shutdown, how do you feel about backing up?
How do you feel about providing more love, support, and understanding?

As I described the different ways shutdown can present itself in others, did you notice any judgments in your mind? How do those judgments carry into your relationships with the people you know in shutdown?

blocks.p: I know you care about the person in shutdown in your life, and I know you're trying to learn everything you can. So great job on this leg of your journey. I hope you keep it going, and I hope you reflect on yourself as well.
